Trillium decumbens is a distinctive southeastern species with a short, trailing rhizome that lies along the soil surface, producing broad, silver-mottled leaves and a dark maroon-red, upright-to-sessile flower nestled low in the foliage in early spring — a habit unlike the taller, more upright trilliums typically grown. Its low, ground-hugging form and striking mottled foliage make it a specialty collector's plant for a shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland bed, best purchased only from nurseries propagating stock responsibly rather than wild-collected. Plant rhizomes with the trailing growth point close to the soil surface rather than buried deeply, and mulch lightly with leaf litter to protect over winter.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; brook wakerobin is the smallest North American trillium and is best grown in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden where drainage and scale can be closely managed.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; brook wakerobin is the smallest North American trillium and is best grown in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden where drainage and scale can be closely managed. Trillium rivale is a diminutive, highly prized Pacific Northwest species native to streamside seeps in the Siskiyou Mountains, producing tiny mottled or plain green leaves and delicate white to pale pink flowers, often finely speckled with purple-red spots, in early spring. Its jewel-like scale and refined flower make it one of the most sought-after trilliums among alpine and woodland plant collectors, though it demands sharper drainage than most trilliums while still needing consistent moisture during the growing season — a balance best achieved in a raised, gritty, humus-amended bed. Source stock only from reputable nurseries propagating from seed or division, never from wild-collected plants, since natural populations are limited and slow to recover from collection.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf wakerobin is native to damp seepage areas and pine flatwoods and needs steadier moisture than many trillium species, without ever becoming waterlogged.

Trillium pusillum is a small, delicate southeastern species with narrow, plain green leaves and a slender white flower that ages to pink as it matures, blooming in early to mid spring in damp, acidic woodland and flatwoods habitat from Virginia to the Gulf Coast. Its diminutive size and preference for consistently moist, acidic soil suit it to a shaded bog garden edge or damp woodland planting alongside pitcher plants and other wetland natives rather than a typical dry upland trillium bed. As with all trillium, buy only nursery-propagated stock, since several regional populations of this species are considered rare or vulnerable and wild collection is a serious conservation concern.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; long-flowered alumroot has slender, tubular flowers held on taller, more graceful stems than many heuchera species, giving it an airier presence in a woodland border.

Heuchera longiflora is an Appalachian native forming a low mound of softly hairy, rounded, lobed leaves and sending up wiry, branching stems of narrow, elongated, greenish-cream, tubular flowers in summer that hang somewhat bell-like rather than the more open, starry flowers of many other heuchera species. It is valued in native plant gardens for supporting hummingbirds and native bees over a long summer bloom period, and its shade tolerance and mounding habit make it a good textural companion for ferns and Solomon's seal. It is easy to grow under standard heuchera conditions and self-sows modestly in favorable sites.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; largefoot toad lily spreads by rhizome to form a colony over time and blooms reliably later in the season than many perennial garden flowers.

Tricyrtis macropoda is an East Asian woodland species with arching, hairy stems bearing broad, pointed leaves and clusters of intricately speckled, star-shaped, pale purple-and-white flowers with prominent recurved petals held along the upper stem in late summer into fall, resembling small orchids up close. Its late-season bloom extends color in a shaded border well past the point when most shade perennials have finished, pairing beautifully with fall-blooming anemone and toad lily relatives. Give it consistent moisture and rich soil, and mulch to protect the shallow rhizomes over winter in the colder part of its hardiness range.
